column2: San Luis Río Colorado (SLRC) is located in northwestern Sonora, Mexico, adjacent to the Colorado River and the U.S. state of Arizona. Water and wastewater services are provided by the Organismo Operador Municipal de Agua Potable, Alcantarillado y Saneamiento (OOMAPAS).
column3: The city operates a unique wastewater treatment plant (PTAR) with natural recharge via anaerobic oxidation lagoons, and has plans for a conventional treatment plant. Potable water comes from wells tapping the river aquifer.
column4: The existing PTAR discharges about 390 L/s (~8.9 MGD), infiltrating around 10 million m³ of treated water per year into the aquiferhttps://oomapasslrc.gob.mx/noticias/es-planta-tratadora-de-san-luis-unica-en-latinoamerica#:~:text=Y%20es%20que%20el%20sistema,actualmente%20en%20todo%20el%20pa%C3%ADs. The system comprises anaerobic lagoons and natural recharge wetlands; it is described as the only such system in Latin Americahttps://oomapasslrc.gob.mx/noticias/es-planta-tratadora-de-san-luis-unica-en-latinoamerica#:~:text=Y%20es%20que%20el%20sistema,actualmente%20en%20todo%20el%20pa%C3%ADs. A proposed project would construct a new wastewater treatment plant with capacity 400 L/s (9.1 MGD) and rehabilitate the sewer systemnadbank.org/hubfs/proyectos/resumen-de-san-luis-rio-colorado.pdf#:~:text=Descripci%C3%B3n%20del%20Proyecto%20y%20Tareas,y%20ampliaci%C3%B3n%20del%20sistema%20de.
column5: The PTAR uses anaerobic and facultative lagoons that promote natural infiltration; treated water supports the Cucapá wetland and irrigates 500 native treeshttps://oomapasslrc.gob.mx/noticias/es-planta-tratadora-de-san-luis-unica-en-latinoamerica#:~:text=c%C3%BAbicos%20al%20a%C3%B1o. OOMAPAS manages operations and reforestation activities. Potable water wells pump to storage tanks and distribution systems.
column6: Effluent quality must meet NOM‑001‑ECOL‑1996. The proposed plant design considered effluent limits for BOD (75 mg/L monthly average), TSS (75 mg/L), nitrogen, phosphorus and metalsnadbank.org/hubfs/proyectos/resumen-de-san-luis-rio-colorado.pdf#:~:text=Descripci%C3%B3n%20del%20Proyecto%20y%20Tareas,por%20ciento%20de%20la%20poblaci%C3%B3n. Drinking water must meet NOM‑127.
column7: Infiltration volume is relatively constant; flows may increase during rainy season. The PTAR supports wetland habitat and reforestation.
column8: No quantitative effluent data; effluent is claimed to match the quality of water extracted from wellshttps://oomapasslrc.gob.mx/noticias/es-planta-tratadora-de-san-luis-unica-en-latinoamerica#:~:text=El%20agua%20se%20devuelve%20al,aves%20migratorias%20y%20una%20gran. Proposed plant design considered limits for temperature (≤40 °C), BOD (≤75 mg/L monthly average), TSS (≤75 mg/L), nitrogen (≤40 mg/L), phosphorus (≤20 mg/L) and metals such as arsenic (≤0.1 mg/L)nadbank.org/hubfs/proyectos/resumen-de-san-luis-rio-colorado.pdf#:~:text=Descripci%C3%B3n%20del%20Proyecto%20y%20Tareas,por%20ciento%20de%20la%20poblaci%C3%B3n.
column9: The lagoon system relies on gravity and natural processes with minimal energy use; new mechanical plants would require pumps and aerators.
column10: Current monitoring likely includes periodic sampling for BOD, TSS and coliforms; proposed plant design anticipated standard laboratory analyses.
column11: Existing system uses anaerobic and facultative lagoons with natural recharge. column2: SLRC is adjacent to the Colorado River; microplastics can originate from urban litter, agricultural plastics and riverine transport.
column3: No studies have reported microplastics in SLRC’s water or wastewater. Due to the natural infiltration system, small particles may be retained in lagoons or recharge wetlands.
column4: No quantitative data; microplastic concentrations are unknown. column8: Mexico does not regulate microplastics; California’s monitoring may set precedent for future cross‑border policies.

column2: SLRC sits along the Colorado River; limited sewer coverage results in significant contamination of the river and aquifer.
column3: The existing sewer network covers only about 37 % of the population, resulting in untreated wastewater being discharged to the Colorado River or septic systems. Contaminants include BOD, TSS, pathogens, nutrients and potentially metals.
column4: The project summary notes that the existing sewer system could not convey community wastewater, leading to spills and stagnant poolsnadbank.org/hubfs/proyectos/resumen-de-san-luis-rio-colorado.pdf#:~:text=gastos%20generados%20por%20la%20comunidad%2C,ciento%20restante%20utiliza%20fosas%20s%C3%A9pticas. column2: Potable water is supplied from wells drawing from the Colorado River aquifer; distribution covers the city and rural areas.
column3: Quality is influenced by natural mineral content and possible contamination from septic systems and agricultural runoff. Public reporting is limited.
column4: No public data on pH, TDS or contaminant levels. Colorado River water typically has TDS ~700 mg/L, hardness ~250 mg/L and nitrate ~2 mg/L.
column5: OOMAPAS pumps groundwater, disinfects with chlorine, and stores water in tanks. System leaks and illegal connections may compromise quality.
column6: Must meet NOM‑127 standards; compliance reports are not published.
column7: Quality may vary with aquifer conditions and seasonal demand.
column8: Potential parameters of interest: TDS, hardness, nitrate, arsenic and fluoride. Without data, values are estimated from Colorado River water.
column9: Energy used for pumping; natural treatment for wastewater uses minimal energy.
column10: Routine monitoring likely includes chlorine residual and coliforms; no microplastics or PFAS monitoring.
column11: Chlorination for disinfection; proposed new plant would improve wastewater quality and reduce contamination of groundwater.
column12: Limited data, high mineral content, contamination from septic systems, and reliance on Colorado River water.
